title: Love as Attachment
text:
In the mid-1980s, Cindy Hazan and Phillip Shaver at the University of Denver wondered whether the attachment patterns Mary Ainsworth had seen in infants might also appear in adult romantic love. To find out, they placed a "love quiz" in the Rocky Mountain News, a Denver newspaper, and invited readers to mail in their answers. Hundreds did. They later repeated the study with university students.

The key question asked readers which of three short descriptions best fit their feelings in close relationships. One described finding it relatively easy to get close to others and not worrying much about being abandoned. Another described discomfort with closeness and difficulty trusting a partner. The third described wanting to get closer than partners seemed to want, and worrying that a partner did not really love them.

Most respondents chose the first, secure description; about a quarter chose the avoidant one and about a fifth the anxious one, proportions roughly similar to those found among infants. People in each group described their most important love relationship in distinctly different ways, and they also remembered their relationships with their parents differently.

The study launched the large field of adult attachment research.
lesson: The way you love as an adult often echoes what you learned about closeness as a child. Recognizing your pattern is the first step to changing it.
source: Hazan, C., and Shaver, P. (1987). Romantic love conceptualized as an attachment process. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 52(3), 511-524.
caveat: The original measure was a single self-report question, and later research treats attachment as a matter of degree on two dimensions rather than three fixed types.
